items.stem: What is the unit of the moment of a force?
items.answer: N m
items.markingKey: Moment = force (N) × perpendicular distance (m).

items.stem: Explain why it is easier to push a door open at the handle than near the hinges.
items.answer: The handle is further from the pivot, so a smaller force gives the same moment.
items.markingKey: larger distance from pivot [1]; same moment with smaller force [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why pushing along the length of a spanner towards the nut has no turning effect.
items.answer: The line of action passes through the pivot, so the perpendicular distance is zero and the moment is zero.
items.markingKey: line of action through pivot [1]; zero perpendicular distance → zero moment [1] [2]

items.stem: In a spanner tightening a wheel nut, a force of 150 N acts at right angles to the spanner at a perpendicular distance of 0.08 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment of the force.
items.answer: 12 N m
items.markingKey: M = Fd = 150 × 0.08 = 12 N m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In a tap being turned, a force of 40 N acts at right angles to the tap handle, 40 cm from the pivot. Calculate the moment in N m.
items.answer: 16 N m

items.stem: Consider a bicycle pedal crank. (a) A force of 80 N is applied at right angles to the crank, 0.25 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment. (b) Suggest one change to the design to make the job easier.
items.answer: (a) 20 N m (b) A longer crank / handle, so a smaller force gives the same moment.
items.markingKey: (a) M = Fd [1] = 20 N m [1] [2] (b) A longer crank / handle [1]; so a smaller force gives the same moment [1] [2]

items.stem: The moment of a force about a pivot is …
options: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force
items.answer: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force
items.markingKey: Moment = F × d, with d perpendicular to the line of action.

items.stem: Explain why a wheelbarrow makes it easier to lift a heavy load.
items.answer: The handles are much further from the pivot (wheel) than the load, so a small upward force on the handles gives a moment equal to that of the load.
items.markingKey: pivot at wheel [1]; larger distance for effort [1] [2]

items.stem: A force is applied at an angle to a spanner rather than at 90°. Explain why the turning effect is smaller.
items.answer: Only the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action counts; at an angle this distance is less than the length of the spanner.
items.markingKey: perpendicular distance [1]; smaller than full length [1] [2]

items.stem: Kwame calculates the moment of a 30 N force acting 50 cm from a pivot as 1500 N m. Identify the error and give the correct value.
items.answer: Kwame did not convert cm to m; M = 30 × 0.5 = 15 N m.
items.markingKey: unit error (cm not converted) [1]; 15 N m [1] [2]

items.stem: Noah calculates the moment of a 30 N force acting 20 cm from a pivot as 600 N m. Identify the error and give the correct value.
items.answer: Noah did not convert cm to m; M = 30 × 0.2 = 6 N m.
items.markingKey: unit error (cm not converted) [1]; 6 N m [1] [2]

items.stem: In a bicycle pedal crank, a force of 40 N acts at right angles to the crank at a perpendicular distance of 0.12 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment of the force.
items.answer: 4.8 N m
items.markingKey: M = Fd = 40 × 0.12 = 4.8 N m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A moment of 18 N m is needed for a door being pushed open. The force is applied at right angles, 30 cm from the pivot. Calculate the force needed.

A moment of 8 N m is needed for a crowbar lifting a paving slab. (a) Calculate the force needed at right angles 10 cm from the pivot. (b) Calculate the force needed if it is applied 25 cm from the pivot. (c) Explain why the force must be at right angles to the crowbar for the answers to be correct.
items.answer: (a) 80 N (b) 32 N (c) the moment uses the perpendicular distance; at another angle the perpendicular distance is less so more force is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 8/0.1 = 80 N [1] (b) 8/0.25 = 32 N [1] (c) perpendicular distance [1]; smaller at other angles [1] [4]

items.stem: Consider a bicycle pedal crank. (a) Calculate the force needed to give the same moment at 0.6 m from the pivot. (b) Suggest one change to the design to make the job easier.
items.answer: (a) 40 N (b) A longer crank / handle, so a smaller force gives the same moment.
items.markingKey: (a) F = 24/0.6 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 40 N with unit [1] [2] (b) A longer crank / handle [1]; so a smaller force gives the same moment [1] [2]

items.stem: Consider a steering wheel. (a) Calculate the force needed to give the same moment at 0.4 m from the pivot. (b) Explain why a force applied at 45° to the wheel rim at the same point has a smaller moment. (c) Suggest one change to the design to make the job easier.
items.answer: (a) 40 N (b) The perpendicular distance to the line of action is less than the full distance. (c) A longer wheel rim / handle, so a smaller force gives the same moment.
items.markingKey: (a) F = 16/0.4 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 40 N with unit [1] [2] (b) The perpendicular distance to the line of action is less than the full distance (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (c) A longer wheel rim / handle [1]; so a smaller force gives the same moment [1] [2]

items.stem: An object is in equilibrium when …
options: it is moving in a circle
the clockwise moments are larger than the anticlockwise moments
there is no resultant force only
there is no resultant force and no resultant moment
items.answer: there is no resultant force and no resultant moment
items.markingKey: Both conditions are needed.

items.stem: Explain how a light child can balance a heavy adult on a see-saw.
items.answer: The child sits further from the pivot so that child’s weight × distance equals adult’s weight × distance.
items.markingKey: moments equal [1]; child further from pivot [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe an experiment to verify the principle of moments using a metre rule.
items.answer: Balance a metre rule on a pivot at its centre; hang known weights at measured distances on both sides until it balances; compare Σ(clockwise F × d) with Σ(anticlockwise F × d) for several arrangements.
items.markingKey: balanced rule on pivot [1]; weights at measured distances [1]; compare sums of moments [1] [3]

items.stem: On a uniform metre rule balanced at its centre, load P of weight 5 N is 15 cm from the pivot on one side. Load Q of weight 0.5 N is on the other side. The system balances. Calculate the distance of load Q from the pivot.
items.answer: 150 cm
items.markingKey: 5 × 15 = 0.5 × d; d = 75/0.5 = 150 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: On a beam balance in a market in Doha, a bag of spices of weight 4 N is 12 cm from the pivot on one side. A set of brass weights of weight 2 N is on the other side. Calculate how far from the pivot a set of brass weights must be for balance, and state the principle you used.
items.answer: 24 cm; principle of moments (clockwise = anticlockwise).
items.markingKey: principle of moments [1]; 4 × 12 = 2 × d [1]; d = 24 cm [1] [3]

items.stem: On a crane jib balanced on its tower, the load of weight 15 kN is 15 m from the pivot on one side. The counterweight of weight 40 kN is on the other side. A further object of weight 5 kN is then placed 11.3 m from the pivot on the same side as the load. (a) Calculate the total anticlockwise moment on that side. (b) Calculate the new distance of the counterweight from the pivot for balance. (c) State the force exerted by the pivot (ignore the weight of the beam).
items.answer: (a) 281 kN m (b) 7.03 m (c) 60 kN upwards

items.stem: Chloe (weight 400 N) and Leila (weight 350 N) sit on a see-saw pivoted at its centre. Chloe sits 1.0 m from the pivot. (a) Leila first sits at the balancing position and then moves 0.2 m further out. Describe and explain what happens. (b) Explain why the weight of a uniform see-saw pivoted at its centre does not affect the balance.
items.answer: (a) Leila’s side goes down: Leila’s moment is now larger than Chloe’s. (b) Its weight acts at the pivot, so it has no moment about the pivot.
items.markingKey: (a) Leila’s side goes down [1]; Leila’s moment is now larger than Chloe’s [1] [2] (b) Its weight acts at the pivot [1]; so it has no moment about the pivot [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel (weight 500 N) and Jonas (weight 250 N) sit on a see-saw pivoted at its centre. Daniel sits 1.0 m from the pivot. (a) Calculate the moment of Daniel’s weight about the pivot. (b) Calculate where Jonas must sit to balance. (c) State the size and direction of the force from the pivot when balanced (ignore the see-saw’s weight).
items.answer: (a) 500 N m (b) 2 m from the pivot on the other side (c) 750 N upwards
items.markingKey: (a) 500 N m [1] (b) principle of moments [1]; answer [1] [2] (c) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 750 N upwards with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A 2 N weight hangs 30 cm to the left of a pivot. Where must a 3 N weight hang to balance it?
options: 20 cm to the right of the pivot
items.answer: 20 cm to the right of the pivot

items.stem: In the principle of moments, for a balanced object …
options: sum of forces up = sum of moments
sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments
items.answer: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments
items.markingKey: Principle of moments about any point.

items.stem: A uniform plank rests on two supports. Explain why the support nearer to a heavy box on the plank pushes up with the greater force.
items.answer: Taking moments about the other support, the box’s moment is large and must be balanced by the nearer support; the box is closer to it so it carries more of the load.
items.markingKey: moments about one support [1]; nearer support carries more [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why both conditions (no resultant force and no resultant moment) are needed for equilibrium.
items.answer: Without resultant force the object could still rotate if moments are unbalanced; without balanced moments it would start to turn.
items.markingKey: force condition prevents acceleration [1]; moment condition prevents rotation [1] [2]

items.stem: A metre rule pivoted at its centre has 5 N hanging 30 cm to the left and 6 N hanging 28 cm to the right. Determine whether it balances; if not, state which way it turns and explain.
items.answer: It does not balance: anticlockwise 150 N cm vs clockwise 168 N cm, so it turns clockwise (right side down).
items.markingKey: both moments calculated [1]; comparison and conclusion [1] [2]

items.stem: A metre rule pivoted at its centre has 5 N hanging 40 cm to the left and 8 N hanging 25 cm to the right. Determine whether it balances; if not, state which way it turns and explain.
items.answer: It balances: both moments are equal (200 N cm).
items.markingKey: both moments calculated [1]; comparison and conclusion [1] [2]

items.stem: On a mobile hanging from a ceiling, a toy bird of weight 1 N is 30 cm from the pivot on one side. A toy fish of weight 2 N is on the other side. The system balances. What is the distance of a toy fish from the pivot?
items.answer: 15 cm

items.stem: On a crane jib balanced on its tower, the load of weight 20 kN is 24 m from the pivot on one side. The counterweight of weight 40 kN is on the other side. The system balances. Calculate the distance of the counterweight from the pivot.
items.markingKey: 20 × 24 = 40 × d; d = 480/40 = 12 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: On a mobile hanging from a ceiling, a toy bird of weight 1.5 N is 40 cm from the pivot on one side. A toy fish of weight 2.5 N is on the other side. The system balances. Calculate the distance of a toy fish from the pivot.
items.answer: 24 cm
items.markingKey: 1.5 × 40 = 2.5 × d; d = 60/2.5 = 24 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: On a crane jib balanced on its tower, the load of weight 12 kN is 18 m from the pivot on one side. The counterweight of weight 50 kN is on the other side. The system balances. Calculate the distance of the counterweight from the pivot.
items.markingKey: 12 × 18 = 50 × d; d = 216/50 = 4.32 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A uniform scaffold board of length 3 m and weight 200 N rests on supports A and B at its two ends. A load of 300 N is placed 2.4 m from A. (a) Take moments about A to find the upward force at B. (b) Find the upward force at A.

A uniform plank of length 2 m and weight 200 N rests on supports A and B at its two ends. A load of 300 N is placed 0.5 m from A. (a) Take moments about A to find the upward force at B. (b) Find the upward force at A.

Hana (weight 300 N) and Sipho (weight 450 N) sit on a see-saw pivoted at its centre. Hana sits 1.5 m from the pivot. (a) Sipho first sits at the balancing position and then moves 0.2 m further out. Describe and explain what happens. (b) Explain why the weight of a uniform see-saw pivoted at its centre does not affect the balance.
items.answer: (a) Sipho’s side goes down: Sipho’s moment is now larger than Hana’s. (b) Its weight acts at the pivot, so it has no moment about the pivot.
items.markingKey: (a) Sipho’s side goes down [1]; Sipho’s moment is now larger than Hana’s [1] [2] (b) Its weight acts at the pivot [1]; so it has no moment about the pivot [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas (weight 500 N) and Felix (weight 250 N) sit on a see-saw pivoted at its centre. Jonas sits 1.2 m from the pivot. (a) Calculate where Felix must sit to balance. (b) Felix first sits at the balancing position and then moves 0.2 m further out. Describe and explain what happens.
items.answer: (a) 2.4 m from the pivot on the other side (b) Felix’s side goes down: Felix’s moment is now larger than Jonas’s.
items.markingKey: (a) principle of moments [1]; answer [1] [2] (b) Felix’s side goes down [1]; Felix’s moment is now larger than Jonas’s [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana (weight 500 N) and Ravi (weight 450 N) sit on a see-saw pivoted at its centre. Ana sits 1.0 m from the pivot. (a) Calculate the moment of Ana’s weight about the pivot. (b) Calculate where Ravi must sit to balance. (c) Ravi first sits at the balancing position and then moves 0.2 m further out. Describe and explain what happens.
items.answer: (a) 500 N m (b) 1.11 m from the pivot on the other side (c) Ravi’s side goes down: Ravi’s moment is now larger than Ana’s.
items.markingKey: (a) 500 N m [1] (b) principle of moments [1]; answer [1] [2] (c) Ravi’s side goes down [1]; Ravi’s moment is now larger than Ana’s [1] [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the centre of gravity of an object?
options: Always the geometric centre of any object
The point through which its whole weight appears to act
The heaviest part of the object
The point where its mass is zero
items.answer: The point through which its whole weight appears to act
items.markingKey: Weight can be treated as acting at one point.

items.stem: Describe how to find the centre of gravity of an irregularly shaped piece of card.
items.answer: Hang the card freely from a pin through a hole near the edge; hang a plumb line from the pin and mark its line; repeat from another hole; the centre of gravity is where the lines cross.
items.markingKey: suspend freely from a point [1]; plumb line marked [1]; repeat; intersection [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a racing car is built low and wide.
items.answer: Low centre of gravity and wide wheelbase mean the line of action of the weight stays inside the base even when tilted on bends, so it is less likely to topple.
items.markingKey: low CG [1]; wide base [1]; line of action stays inside base [1] [3]

items.stem: A lamp has a base 2 m wide and its centre of gravity is 1.2 m above the centre of the base. It is tilted about one edge by 40°. Its critical angle is 39.8°. State whether it falls over and explain.
items.answer: It topples: the tilt is more than 39.8°, so the line of action of the weight is outside the base.
items.markingKey: decision [1]; line of action vs base [1] [2]

items.stem: A tractor on a hillside has a base 2 m wide and its centre of gravity is 4 m above the centre of the base. Calculate the angle through which it can be tilted about one edge before it topples.
items.markingKey: topples when CG is vertically above the edge [1]; tan θ = 1/4 [1]; θ = 14° [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider a stacking robot with a base 0.6 m wide and its centre of gravity 1.5 m above the centre of the base. (a) State what is meant by its centre of gravity. (b) Calculate the maximum angle it can be tilted before toppling. (c) It is tilted slightly about one bottom edge. Calculate the moment of its 300 N weight about that edge when the weight acts 0.1 m horizontally inside the edge.
items.answer: (a) The point through which its weight appears to act. (b) 11.3° (c) 30 N m
items.markingKey: (a) The point through which its weight appears to act [1] (b) tan θ = 0.3/1.5 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 11.3° with unit [1] [2] (c) 300 × 0.1: 30 N m [1]

items.stem: Which change makes a bus more stable?
items.answer: Lowering its centre of gravity
items.markingKey: Low centre of gravity and wide base increase stability.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which apparatus is used to find the centre of gravity of an irregular flat card? (b) Which change makes a bus more stable?
items.answer: (a) A plumb line and a pin (b) Lowering its centre of gravity
items.markingKey: (a) Hang the card from a pin and draw the vertical plumb line from two or more points. (b) Low centre of gravity and wide base increase stability.

items.stem: Explain why a tall glass of water is more likely to fall over than a short wide one.
items.answer: The tall glass has a higher centre of gravity and narrower base, so a smaller tilt moves the line of action of the weight outside the base.
items.markingKey: higher CG / narrower base [1]; smaller tilt needed to move weight outside base [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain, using moments, why a tilted object falls back to its original position if the line of action of its weight is inside the base.
items.answer: The weight then has a moment about the edge of the base that turns the object back towards its original position.
items.markingKey: weight’s moment about pivot edge [1]; restoring direction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a person carrying a heavy bag in one hand leans the other way.
items.answer: Leaning moves the combined centre of gravity back over the feet (base), so the line of action of the weight stays within the base.
items.markingKey: combined CG [1]; kept over feet / base [1] [2]

items.stem: A lamp has a base 1 m wide and its centre of gravity is 1.25 m above the centre of the base. It is tilted about one edge by 15°. Its critical angle is 21.8°. State whether it falls over and explain.
items.answer: It falls back: the tilt is less than 21.8°, so the line of action of the weight is inside the base.
items.markingKey: decision [1]; line of action vs base [1] [2]

items.stem: A filing cabinet has a base 1.6 m wide and its centre of gravity is 2.4 m above the centre of the base. It is tilted about one edge by 20°. Its critical angle is 18.4°. State whether it falls over and explain.
items.answer: It topples: the tilt is more than 18.4°, so the line of action of the weight is outside the base.
items.markingKey: decision [1]; line of action vs base [1] [2]

items.stem: A wooden block has a base 0.5 m wide and its centre of gravity is 0.75 m above the centre of the base. Calculate the angle through which it can be tilted about one edge before it topples.
items.markingKey: topples when CG is vertically above the edge [1]; tan θ = 0.25/0.75 [1]; θ = 18.4° [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider a stacking robot with a base 1 m wide and its centre of gravity 0.8 m above the centre of the base. (a) Calculate the maximum angle it can be tilted before toppling. (b) Explain why it returns to upright when released from a small tilt.
items.answer: (a) 32° (b) The weight acts inside the base, giving a moment about the edge that turns it back.
items.markingKey: (a) tan θ = 0.5/0.8 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 32° with unit [1] [2] (b) The weight acts inside the base [1]; giving a moment about the edge that turns it back [1] [2]

items.stem: Consider a tall cupboard with a base 1 m wide and its centre of gravity 1.2 m above the centre of the base. (a) Calculate the maximum angle it can be tilted before toppling. (b) It is tilted slightly about one bottom edge. Calculate the moment of its 800 N weight about that edge when the weight acts 0.1 m horizontally inside the edge. (c) Suggest two ways to make it harder to topple.
items.answer: (a) 22.6° (b) 80 N m (c) Lower the centre of gravity (heavy items at the bottom); widen the base.
items.markingKey: (a) tan θ = 0.5/1.2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 22.6° with unit [1] [2] (b) 800 × 0.1: 80 N m [1] (c) Lower the centre of gravity (heavy items at the bottom) [1]; widen the base [1] [2]

items.stem: Suggest and explain two design features that make a baby’s high chair stable.
items.answer: Wide base (feet spread out) and low centre of gravity (heavy base / weight kept low), so the line of action of the weight stays within the base when it is tilted.
items.markingKey: wide base with reason [1]; low CG with reason [1]; link to line of action of weight within base [1] [3]

items.stem: A tractor on a hillside has a base 2 m wide and its centre of gravity is 2.5 m above the centre of the base. It is tilted about one edge by 25°. Its critical angle is 21.8°. State whether it falls over and explain.
items.answer: It topples: the tilt is more than 21.8°, so the line of action of the weight is outside the base.
items.markingKey: decision [1]; line of action vs base [1] [2]

items.stem: A filing cabinet has a base 0.8 m wide and its centre of gravity is 1.2 m above the centre of the base. Calculate the angle through which it can be tilted about one edge before it topples.
items.markingKey: topples when CG is vertically above the edge [1]; tan θ = 0.4/1.2 [1]; θ = 18.4° [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider a delivery lorry with a base 1 m wide and its centre of gravity 1.2 m above the centre of the base. (a) Calculate the maximum angle it can be tilted before toppling. (b) Explain why it returns to upright when released from a small tilt. (c) Suggest two ways to make it harder to topple.
items.answer: (a) 22.6° (b) The weight acts inside the base, giving a moment about the edge that turns it back. (c) Lower the centre of gravity (heavy items at the bottom); widen the base.
items.markingKey: (a) tan θ = 0.5/1.2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 22.6° with unit [1] [2] (b) The weight acts inside the base [1]; giving a moment about the edge that turns it back [1] [2] (c) Lower the centre of gravity (heavy items at the bottom) [1]; widen the base [1] [2]

items.stem: Which change makes it easier to undo a tight nut with a spanner?
options: Pushing along the handle towards the nut
items.answer: Using a longer spanner
items.markingKey: Greater distance gives a greater moment for the same force.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A force is applied at an angle to a spanner rather than at 90°. Explain why the turning effect is smaller. (b) Explain why pushing along the length of a spanner towards the nut has no turning effect.
items.answer: (a) Only the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action counts; at an angle this distance is less than the length of the spanner. (b) The line of action passes through the pivot, so the perpendicular distance is zero and the moment is zero.
items.markingKey: (a) perpendicular distance [1]; smaller than full length [1] [2] (b) line of action through pivot [1]; zero perpendicular distance → zero moment [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A force is applied at an angle to a spanner rather than at 90°. Explain why the turning effect is smaller. (b) Explain why a wheelbarrow makes it easier to lift a heavy load.
items.answer: (a) Only the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action counts; at an angle this distance is less than the length of the spanner. (b) The handles are much further from the pivot (wheel) than the load, so a small upward force on the handles gives a moment equal to that of the load.
items.markingKey: (a) perpendicular distance [1]; smaller than full length [1] [2] (b) pivot at wheel [1]; larger distance for effort [1] [2]

items.stem: In a pair of scissors cutting card, a force of 25 N acts at right angles to the scissors at a perpendicular distance of 0.1 m from the pivot. Work out the moment of the force.
items.answer: 2.5 N m
items.markingKey: M = Fd = 25 × 0.1 = 2.5 N m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A moment of 2.25 N m is needed for a steering wheel. The force is applied at right angles, 15 cm from the pivot. Calculate the force needed.

Consider a bicycle pedal crank. (a) A force of 80 N is applied at right angles to the crank, 0.3 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment. (b) Explain why a force applied at 45° to the crank at the same point has a smaller moment.
items.answer: (a) 24 N m (b) The perpendicular distance to the line of action is less than the full distance.

items.stem: State the principle of moments.
items.answer: For an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.
items.markingKey: sum clockwise = sum anticlockwise [1]; about the same point, in equilibrium [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why both conditions (no resultant force and no resultant moment) are needed for equilibrium. (b) A uniform plank rests on two supports. Explain why the support nearer to a heavy box on the plank pushes up with the greater force.
items.answer: (a) Without resultant force the object could still rotate if moments are unbalanced; without balanced moments it would start to turn. (b) Taking moments about the other support, the box’s moment is large and must be balanced by the nearer support; the box is closer to it so it carries more of the load.
items.markingKey: (a) force condition prevents acceleration [1]; moment condition prevents rotation [1] [2] (b) moments about one support [1]; nearer support carries more [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why both conditions (no resultant force and no resultant moment) are needed for equilibrium. (b) Explain how a light child can balance a heavy adult on a see-saw.
items.answer: (a) Without resultant force the object could still rotate if moments are unbalanced; without balanced moments it would start to turn. (b) The child sits further from the pivot so that child’s weight × distance equals adult’s weight × distance.
items.markingKey: (a) force condition prevents acceleration [1]; moment condition prevents rotation [1] [2] (b) moments equal [1]; child further from pivot [1] [2]

items.stem: On a crane jib balanced on its tower, the load of weight 12 kN is 20 m from the pivot on one side. The counterweight of weight 40 kN is on the other side. The system balances. Determine the distance of the counterweight from the pivot.
items.answer: 6 m
items.markingKey: 12 × 20 = 40 × d; d = 240/40 = 6 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: On a beam balance in a market in Bogotá, a bag of spices of weight 2 N is 24 cm from the pivot on one side. A set of brass weights of weight 4 N is on the other side. The system balances. Work out the distance of a set of brass weights from the pivot.
items.answer: 12 cm
items.markingKey: 2 × 24 = 4 × d; d = 48/4 = 12 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: On a uniform metre rule balanced at its centre, load P of weight 4 N is 24 cm from the pivot on one side. Load Q of weight 3 N is on the other side. The system balances. Determine the distance of load Q from the pivot.
items.answer: 32 cm
items.markingKey: 4 × 24 = 3 × d; d = 96/3 = 32 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Felix (weight 500 N) and Hana (weight 350 N) sit on a see-saw pivoted at its centre. Felix sits 1.5 m from the pivot. (a) Hana first sits at the balancing position and then moves 0.2 m further out. Describe and explain what happens. (b) Explain why the weight of a uniform see-saw pivoted at its centre does not affect the balance.
items.answer: (a) Hana’s side goes down: Hana’s moment is now larger than Felix’s. (b) Its weight acts at the pivot, so it has no moment about the pivot.
items.markingKey: (a) Hana’s side goes down [1]; Hana’s moment is now larger than Felix’s [1] [2] (b) Its weight acts at the pivot [1]; so it has no moment about the pivot [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf (weight 300 N) and Freya (weight 250 N) sit on a see-saw pivoted at its centre. Yusuf sits 1.0 m from the pivot. (a) Calculate the moment of Yusuf’s weight about the pivot. (c) Explain why the weight of a uniform see-saw pivoted at its centre does not affect the balance.
items.answer: (a) 300 N m (b) 550 N upwards (c) Its weight acts at the pivot, so it has no moment about the pivot.
